document.title: Open Cognitive Bubbles — Deep Concept, Research, and Validation Plan
document.purpose: Explain the Open Cognitive Bubbles concept deeply enough for research, technical sparring, prototyping, and falsification. This document treats the idea as a hypothesis to test, not a product assumption.
document.source_basis: Developed from the prior Open Cognitive Bubbles concept and subsequent critical sparring around collective memory, AI-mediated context coordination, provenance, privacy, and human-AI collaboration.

executive_summary.core_problem: AI is increasingly extending individual cognition, but collaboration tools still assume that useful context must be manually copied into a centralized shared surface. This creates a gap between rich private AI-extended thinking and comparatively impoverished communal problem solving.
executive_summary.core_hypothesis: People may be able to contribute more useful knowledge to shared problems if they can selectively open governed apertures from independently controlled AI-extended cognitive environments into a persistent shared problem space.
executive_summary.one_line: Private augmented cognition + governed apertures + persistent shared problem memory.
executive_summary.strongest_formulation: A governed interface through which independently controlled, AI-extended human cognition can participate in persistent communal problem solving.
executive_summary.what_is_potentially_new: The potentially distinctive interaction is not shared AI memory by itself. It is multiple independently controlled human+AI cognitive environments selectively interoperating around a shared problem while preserving attribution, disclosure boundaries, plural interpretations, and human authority.
executive_summary.key_unknown: Can useful knowledge cross the aperture with low enough friction, high enough trust, and sufficient privacy to outperform ordinary shared chat or centralized AI collaboration?

current_pattern: Individuals increasingly use personal AI assistants with access to their own notes, documents, code, research, memory, and preferences.
These private AI environments may contain far richer context than what is visible in a group chat, meeting, or shared document.
To collaborate, people currently have to decide manually what to copy, summarize, disclose, or explain.
Useful weak signals, unfinished thoughts, doubts, partial expertise, and relevant private materials often never cross into the shared space.
Centralizing all private context into one shared AI would simplify retrieval but introduces unacceptable privacy, ownership, trust, governance, and autonomy problems.
problem_statement.design_question: Can collaboration benefit from private AI-extended cognition without requiring all private context, memory, tools, and models to be centralized?
secondary_questions: Can an AI reveal that relevant knowledge exists without revealing the knowledge itself?
Can different people use different AI systems while still contributing interoperable objects?
Can shared reasoning preserve disagreement and provenance instead of collapsing everything into a single synthesis?
Can collective memory remain useful without becoming a transcript swamp?
What immediate personal benefit motivates participants to open their cognitive bubble?

cognitive_bubble.definition: A personally or institutionally controlled augmented cognition environment.
cognitive_bubble.important_property: The cognitive bubble is not automatically part of the shared system. It remains independently controlled.

shared_problem_space.definition: A persistent environment organized around a problem, question, or challenge rather than around a single organization, application, group chat, or AI assistant.
shared_problem_space.important_property: The shared problem space does not need to own the participants' full private memories or AI environments.

aperture.definition: A governed, revocable, and inspectable boundary between a cognitive bubble and a shared problem space.
aperture.why_it_matters: The aperture is the key trust and interoperability primitive. It defines what another human, AI, or shared problem space may learn, ask, infer, publish, or reuse.
control_dimensions: which problem spaces may interact with the bubble
what categories of private sources may be consulted
whether only relevance may be revealed
whether source identity may be revealed
whether participant identity may be revealed
whether AI may prepare a contribution

contribution.definition: A bounded, attributable object deliberately exposed to the shared problem space.
contribution.key_rule: A contribution is not equivalent to the person's complete belief, memory, or private context.

problem_memory.definition: The diachronic accumulation of shared contributions, relationships, provenance, disagreements, evaluations, and changes around a problem.
problem_memory.truth_model: Problem memory should represent attributed assertions and governance status, not one universal canonical truth.
example: Person B disputed X using evidence E.
Working group Y provisionally accepted X under condition C.
Experiment Z later contradicted assumption A.

current_collaboration.limitation: Participants must manually externalize useful context and often leave private AI-assisted reasoning disconnected from the group.

personal_copilot.limitation: Each participant gains augmentation, but the augmentations remain informational islands.

open_cognitive_bubbles.shape: Human <-> personal AI/cognitive bubble <-> governed aperture <-> shared problem memory <-> apertures <-> other cognitive bubbles
open_cognitive_bubbles.distinctive_property: Each participant has an individual doorway into communal reasoning without surrendering their entire private context.

participation_model.name: availability_signal
participation_model.meaning: The bubble may reveal that relevant knowledge, experience, or capacity might exist without revealing the underlying content.

participation_model.name: mediated_query
participation_model.meaning: The shared problem may submit bounded questions. The bubble decides whether and how to respond.

participation_model.name: reviewed_contribution
participation_model.meaning: AI may draft a contribution, but the participant reviews the exact outbound object before publication.

participation_model.name: bounded_delegation
participation_model.meaning: The participant authorizes AI to monitor or contribute within explicit scopes, rate limits, provenance rules, and revocable permissions.

authorship_provenance_model.principle: AI generation, human review, publication authority, endorsement, and institutional authority must remain distinct.
authorship_provenance_model.critical_rule: Never transform 'Person A said X' into 'X is true' without an explicit governance transition.

aperture_contract_hypothesis.why_first: The aperture is the part of the concept that is most distinctive and most likely to fail. It should be specified and tested before building a full decentralized memory protocol.
aperture_contract_hypothesis.core_security_principle: Aperture enforcement must happen before information enters a shared model context. Privacy cannot depend solely on instructing an LLM not to disclose restricted information.

key_novel_interaction.name: permission-safe latent overlap discovery
scenario: Participant A privately writes that ownership is the real problem.
Participant B independently expresses a similar concern privately.
Each participant may receive a message such as: 'Another participant appears to be exploring a closely related concern. Would you like to make your concern discoverable?'
Only after consent does additional information cross the aperture.
key_novel_interaction.why_it_matters: This could make latent distributed knowledge available to a group without requiring every tentative thought to be published.
why_it_is_dangerous: Users may experience it as surveillance.
Even revealing that an overlap exists can disclose sensitive information.
The system may infer false similarity.
Social power differences may make disclosure feel coerced.
Participants may not understand what the AI inferred from their private context.

not: one centralized AI with everyone's private data
instead: shared problem memory that persists beyond individual conversations

technical_architecture_v0.goal: Test the interaction and trust model with the least infrastructure possible.

components.frontend: Simple web app with one private workspace per participant and one shared problem view.
components.identity: Local accounts or basic OAuth for prototype; no decentralized identity required initially.
components.vector_search: pgvector or equivalent for semantic relevance and overlap candidates.
components.private_memory: Separate per-participant namespaces or stores enforced deterministically.
components.event_log: Append-oriented event table in PostgreSQL; Kafka is not required for prototype.
components.llm: One or more model adapters behind a small tool interface.
components.policy_engine: Deterministic aperture rules applied before model-visible context assembly.
components.audit_log: Record every attempted and actual disclosure across apertures.

defer: cryptographic signing beyond what is necessary for prototype

if_v0_succeeds: encrypted or permissioned shared problem spaces

possible_atproto_role.limitations: ATProto does not itself solve private working memory, governance, consensus, model provenance, confidential inference, or scientific auditability.

phase_0_concept_attack.goal: Determine whether the concept is materially distinct from shared RAG, AI group chat, organizational memory, CSCW systems, and agent blackboards.
activities: Review CSCW and organizational memory literature.
Review argumentation systems and IBIS-style tools.
Review privacy-preserving collaborative AI and federated-agent research.
Review blackboard architectures and multi-agent shared-state systems.
Review personal AI memory products and shared AI workspaces.
Review decentralized social/protocol work around ATProto permissioned spaces and groups.
Map closest commercial and open-source analogues.
phase_0_concept_attack.decision_gate: Continue only if the governed aperture or independently controlled cognitive-bubble topology creates a testable distinction beyond existing shared-memory collaboration.

phase_1_aperture_specification.goal: Define exactly what crosses between private and shared cognition.
activities: Write threat models for inference attacks.
phase_1_aperture_specification.decision_gate: Do not prototype multi-user mediation until participants can understand and predict the aperture rules.

phase_2_static_simulation.goal: Test the UX and privacy model before connecting live LLMs to real private data.
phase_2_static_simulation.setup: Four simulated participants with hand-authored private and shared contributions.
activities: Test participant comprehension with scenario walkthroughs.
success_criteria: Users correctly predict what will and will not be disclosed.
Users understand the difference between relevance signal, synthesis, quotation, and publication.
Provenance is understandable without becoming overwhelming.

phase_3_live_micro_experiment.goal: Test whether participants actually contribute more useful latent knowledge through private AI interaction.
phase_3_live_micro_experiment.problem: One bounded problem with enough distributed knowledge and uncertainty to make collaboration meaningful.
conditions: Experimental B: private AI workspaces + shared problem memory + reviewed apertures.
metrics: number of contributions participants report they would not have posted directly
reuse of contributions later in the experiment
qualitative_questions: Did the system surface something you would not have found manually?
Did you share something you would not have put into the group chat?
Did any system intervention feel creepy or surveillance-like?
Did you understand what your AI was allowed to reveal?
Did the shared memory help you think, or did it add administrative overhead?
phase_3_live_micro_experiment.decision_gate: Continue only if experimental collaboration produces clearly useful context or participation that the shared-chat baseline misses.

phase_4_real_domain_pilot.goal: Test the model in a real collaborative setting where provenance and distributed expertise matter.
candidate_domains: expert network tackling a bounded policy or technical problem
phase_4_real_domain_pilot.deliverable: Real-world field report and revised aperture contract.

phase_5_interoperability_test.goal: Determine whether independent AI environments can participate through a shared protocol rather than one application.
activities: Allow different model providers or local models.
Evaluate ATProto or another federated substrate.
phase_5_interoperability_test.decision_gate: Only pursue protocol work if users value cross-environment participation enough to justify interoperability complexity.

prototype_plan.prototype_goal: Demonstrate that independently controlled personal AI contexts can produce useful shared contributions without centralizing private memory.
user_flow: Participant enters a private note or source.
Personal AI uses only that participant's private scope.
Shared problem asks or exposes a current subquestion.
System checks whether the participant's bubble contains potentially relevant context.
Depending on aperture policy, the bubble returns nothing, a relevance signal, a candidate synthesis, or a proposed contribution.
If review is required, the participant sees exactly what will leave the bubble.
The approved contribution enters shared memory with provenance.
Other participants' AIs receive relevant shared contributions according to their own context.
The system may identify possible cross-participant overlap and ask for consent before stronger disclosure.
The shared problem view shows plural contributions and contradictions without forcing consensus.

baseline.name: Shared Chat
baseline.description: All participants receive the same problem and source access appropriate to the baseline. They collaborate in one shared chat with an AI assistant.

experimental.name: Cognitive Bubbles
experimental.description: Each participant has private AI-assisted context plus governed apertures and a persistent shared contribution space.

primary_outcomes: quality of final shared problem understanding
falsification_conditions: shared chat performs equally well with lower complexity
participants do not trust overlap detection
AI cannot produce useful bounded contributions without revealing too much private context
shared memory accumulates noise faster than reusable knowledge
participants cannot predict what crosses the aperture

threats: re-identification through writing style or rare facts
private-content leakage via embeddings or similarity scores
required_tests: Can an attacker infer private facts through repeated relevance queries?
Can refusal patterns leak knowledge presence?
Can overlap notifications expose sensitive relationships?
Can model prompts bypass aperture policy?
Can users inspect all disclosures after the fact?
Can users revoke future access cleanly?
trust_and_safety_research.design_bias: Prefer less functionality and stronger understandable boundaries over impressive but opaque AI mediation.

memory_hygiene.principle: Shared memory must preserve useful structure without becoming a dump of every AI-generated thought.
rules: Private drafts remain private unless deliberately exposed.
AI-generated candidate contributions are not equivalent to published contributions.
Duplicate and contradiction detection should propose relationships rather than silently merge records.
Superseded and retracted claims remain historically inspectable where appropriate.
The system should support plural and conflicting interpretations.
Participants should be able to distinguish evidence from synthesis and endorsement.

success_story.example: Four researchers are tackling a technical question. One has private notes on a failed experiment, another has domain literature, a third has code from a related project, and a fourth has a half-formed concern they are not ready to state publicly. Their personal AIs identify relevance to a shared subquestion. Each participant reviews a bounded contribution. The shared problem memory surfaces a contradiction between the literature and experiment. A later participant's AI receives that contradiction as relevant context. The group progresses without anyone uploading their entire personal memory into one centralized assistant.
why_better_than_shared_chat: private context can contribute without being fully disclosed
useful contributions become reusable objects rather than buried messages
the system can route shared developments back into each participant's private context

failure_story.example: Participants spend more time configuring permissions and reviewing AI-generated outbound text than solving the problem. Overlap notifications feel invasive. Contributions become redundant summaries. Everyone eventually copies the useful facts into the shared chat because it is simpler.
failure_story.conclusion: If this happens consistently, the aperture architecture does not justify itself.

conceptual: Is a cognitive bubble an actual architectural primitive or only a metaphor for personal AI workspace isolation?
Is the shared problem the correct persistent object?
Does independently controlled cognition create a meaningful new collaboration topology?
ux: What is the minimum control surface needed for users to understand disclosure?
How much provenance should be visible by default?
Do people value a private doorway into shared problems?
When should the system suggest sharing versus remain silent?
technical: Can aperture policies be enforced deterministically across heterogeneous AI environments?
Can semantic overlap detection operate without leaking restricted information?
How should contributions be signed and versioned?
How can independent aggregators disagree without destroying usability?
social: Does mediation improve participation from quieter or lower-status members?
Does it create new forms of surveillance or social pressure?
How does the system preserve minority and dissenting views?
Who governs a shared problem identity?
economic: Who has enough pain to adopt this?
Is the first buyer a research team, institution, community platform, or infrastructure provider?
Is interoperability itself valuable enough to motivate adoption?

continue: participants contribute useful knowledge they would not otherwise have shared
permission-safe mediation creates meaningful cross-person connections
users understand and trust the disclosure model
shared contributions remain useful after the original conversation
the baseline shared chat misses important context
pivot: collective memory is useful but private apertures are too complex
users value decision provenance but not distributed AI environments
users prefer one shared assistant but want stronger attribution and governance
the strongest value appears in a specific vertical such as research collaboration
kill_or_pause: participants consistently prefer ordinary shared chat
privacy-safe mediation removes too much useful information
AI-generated contributions create more noise than signal
maintenance and review cost exceeds coordination benefit

tasks: Define four disclosure modes with concrete examples.
Research CSCW, organizational memory, privacy-preserving collaboration, blackboard systems, and closest AI products.
Build one HTML/React mock with four fake participants.
Implement My Bubble, Shared Problem, and Outbound Review.
Test whether users understand what would be disclosed.
Run shared-chat baseline and bubble condition.
Measure useful hidden knowledge, discovered links, trust, and friction.
Write a falsification report rather than a product roadmap.

requested_llm_sparring.instruction: Treat this as a research hypothesis. Do not optimize the pitch. Try to break it.
questions: Which known academic or commercial systems most closely implement this topology?
Is the governed aperture genuinely distinct from privacy-aware tool calling and access-controlled RAG?
What is the simplest possible architecture that can test the hypothesis?
What kinds of information cannot safely cross an aperture even as an anonymous relevance signal?
Could secure computation, local models, federated retrieval, or cryptographic methods materially improve the model?
What social-science research predicts whether people will trust or reject this?
What bounded collaborative problem is most likely to show a dramatic advantage over shared chat?
What would falsify the concept fastest?
If the concept works, what should become a protocol and what should remain application-specific?
desired_verdict: interesting but primarily a privacy-aware shared-RAG pattern
promising interaction with weak protocol justification
valuable only for specific high-provenance domains
too socially risky or operationally costly

current_conclusion.classification: Interesting communal-computing architecture with a testable but unproven interaction primitive.
current_conclusion.strongest_claim: The possible innovation is not a larger collective AI. It is a governed way for independently controlled, AI-extended human cognition to contribute to shared reasoning without surrendering the whole private cognitive environment.
current_conclusion.highest_priority: Prototype and falsify the aperture contract.
current_conclusion.do_not_do_next: Do not build a full decentralized platform, temporal graph, dynamic UI system, or protocol before demonstrating that people actually value and trust this interaction.
